items.title: Swing and a miss: Paying with Bitcoin on a Square Terminal
items.text:
This year, I've got my kids doing a homeschool co-op two days a week. This just means that a group of homeschool parents have organized to teach their children in a group setting, and possibly hire a teacher or two for subjects where more formal education might be helpful (languages, music, science?). 

Unfortunately, the coop we have joined is quite some way from our home, so after dropping off the children, I go to a nearby coffee shop to work -- a coffee shop that has a Square terminal.

I have asked if they accept Bitcoin a number of times so far, but in all cases the cashier's answer has been "I don't think so" or "I'll have to talk to the person who manages this" (pointing at the terminal). It's a busy place and so there is often a line, and I haven't wanted to try to make anyone wait while I help figure out how to turn on Bitcoin payments, and so I haven't made much progress. 

Today, the person behind the cash register was the owner and I seized my opportunity. 

I placed my order and while he was ringing it up, I said, "I've heard that these Square terminals accept bitcoin."

The owner glanced up at me and said, "I've heard that, too. Let's see if we can figure it out."

This was a much more enthusiastic response than I was expecting. He poked away at the terminal for a few minutes and then said, "I think it only takes bitcoin if you have CashApp."

I told him that this was not the case, but that if he could get it to display a QR code I could try paying that.

He continued to tap on the terminal without much effect. I should say this terminal was not the sort that has a rotatable screen. There is one fixed screen facing the cashier and a smaller fixed screen facing the customer. This was showing the message "Waiting for cashier..."

"I think you have to tap to pay," he said.

Now, I don't use any of the Lightning wallets that have implemented tap to pay (as far as I remember there aren't very many) so that wasn't an option. I told him that I needed a QR code to scan.

After another couple minutes, the owner volunteered: "Maybe I can text it to you." 

I am usually loathe to provide a phone number, but in the interest of dismantling the legacy financial system, I gave it to him. I immediately received a text with a link. The link was to pay for my coffee, but had required fields for name, phone number, and email. At the bottom I saw a green button that said pay with CashApp or something like that. I tapped it, but nothing happened because I had not entered the required fields. 

Still in the interest of taking down the fiat empire, I entered some incorrect information in these fields. But then when I tapped the green button, it presented me with a message informing me that I did not have CashApp and a button to download CashApp. 

At this point the line behind me was long enough that I offered to pay with cash and the owner accept with some visible signs of relief.

So: I have failed on this the fourth time I've tried to pay with Bitcoin at this Square terminal. I suspect that the owner needs to turn Bitcoin payments on and that I will need to talk him through this process, so I'll have to rewatch those videos about how to do this. 

It occurs to me that Square could do a lot better with this flow if they had a button that allowed the cashier to display a QR code that was simultaneously a CashApp code and a Lightning invoice. This is a lot to ask, but I'm pretty sure it needs to be at least that easy for it to work well.

items.title: Guilty until proven innocent
items.text:
ALL surveillance and control, all AML, KYC and all violations of privacy are completely unethical, immoral and illegitimate. All of them! As recently as the 1990s, one could purchase stocks without providing identification. Bank deposits below arbitrary thresholds required no explanation or documentation. Cash transactions, regardless of size, were presumed legitimate unless specific evidence suggested otherwise. The default assumption was that individuals had the right to conduct their financial affairs privately, with the burden of proof resting on authorities to demonstrate wrongdoing before intruding upon that privacy.

This historical norm was not an oversight or a failure of governance, it was a recognition of a fundamental principle. Free societies operate on the presumption of innocence, treating citizens as autonomous agents capable of managing their own affairs unless proven otherwise through due process. The current system inverts this relationship entirely, treating every citizen as a potential criminal whose financial activities must be continuously monitored and pre-approved by state bureaucrats. Given how KYC for everything short of going to a rest room is being normalized, the world needs more privacy protecting tools, not less.

items.title: Is L-BTC a shitcoin?
items.text:
# The closest I've ever come to being a shitcoiner

Back in 2024, I spent a lot of time looking at ecash. Ecash is cool -- it has all these neat properties like potentially better privacy and maybe being a bearer asset like cash and being so lightweight that almost anyone can run a mint and cypherpunks have been working on ecash since long before bitcoin. Development in Cashu and Fedimint was in full flower and there weren't many viable alternatives like Ark or Spark.

@TonyGiorgio wrote a post in January of 2024 called "Fedimint is Self-Custodial" https://stacker.news/items/395461 which was the catalyst for a particular fascination of mine: trying to determine what sort of thing an ecash token actually is. Is it like a gift card? https://stacker.news/items/397764/r/Scoresby or a repurchase agreement a la the Fed's repo window? https://stacker.news/items/565172/r/Scoresby Is it a token you buy? https://stacker.news/items/554143/r/Scoresby

It was clear to me that ecash tokens were not bitcoin, but at that point in Bitcoin culture if a token wasn't bitcoin, it could only be a shitcoin -- and yet I didn't think using ecash was shitcoining. I think this was because I associate shitcoining with scamming and degenerate trading and pump 'n dump schemes while ecash was clearly trying to do payments.

I got so interested in the idea that I believe @Car felt compelled to block me and I recall a number of fiery conversations with @justin_shocknet.

# Justin was right

There were many points about which we disagreed, but I believe one of the most significant was that I tried to defend the use of ecash as less trusting than simply relying on a custodian. About this, I was most certainly wrong. Here is Justin [explaining it to me](https://stacker.news/items/554143/r/Scoresby?commentId=554230):

![](https://m.stacker.news/155829)

# Why the change of mind

That last bit in Justin's comment gets at it. I wanted to think about a mint in isolation or as a complete system, but this is obviously not the case. Ecash mints are an attempt to glue a non-bitcoin system onto bitcoin and so evaluating as some whole thing on its own was not particularly relevant to users who were interested in sats.

This was made painfully clear by the recent Liquid hack. There are 15 "geographically distributed" Liquid functionaries in their federation and at least 11 of them are required to finalize blocks. And yet, almost the entire amount of bitcoin in the Liquid Network was withdrawn and block production was halted.

In that moment, calling a Liquid wallet self-custodial was pretty clearly demonstrated to be wrong. If you have a L-BTC balance in ACQUA Wallet, Manna Wallet, or Misty Breez you can't move your sats (and you may not actually have any sats). Doesn't sound very self-custodial.

This interaction with @Roy_Breez was very enlightening:

![](https://imgprxy.stacker.news/Uv9piRjMpEGZXhf394gOtE-JsUrOj3DSE49enKKft_8/rs:fit:2560:1440/aHR0cHM6Ly9tLnN0YWNrZXIubmV3cy8xNTU3ODU)

![](https://imgprxy.stacker.news/Nen5MnjrhiSPdtgEtJxk1bsSkcl-edx0-smACu0JfwQ/rs:fit:2560:1440/aHR0cHM6Ly9tLnN0YWNrZXIubmV3cy8xNTU3ODY)

We've been calling these things self-custodial, but the users can't use their money and possibly don't even have it any more.

# Okay, but Coldcard users also lost funds out of their wallets...

This may seem like a pedantic point, but it really drove it home for me. The key difference between Coldcard users and Liquid users that makes one self-custodial and the other custodial is that when you open a Liquid-based wallet right now, it still shows your balance...you just don't have it. Both Coldcard users and Liquid users have experienced theft -- but the latter still have their L-BTC and that makes all the difference. Because what value does L-BTC have if there's no BTC in the Liquid Federation wallet? (or even if there's not enough BTC there?)

I wanted to be able to call things like ecash tokens and L-BTC something other than a shitcoin because I thought there was a way for them to be used in lieu of bitcoin, but the reality is that such an approach muddies the water. If we are going to call a bitcoin wallet self-custodial, the bitcoin wallet shouldn't show you a balance when there isn't one.[^1]

# Where does this leave me and my fascination with ecash and other fake L2s?

I don't think L-BTC is a shitcoin. But it ***is*** more accurate to call Liquid *custodial*. Same goes for ecash, Ark, Spark, and all the other fake L2s.

[^1]: And for you jerks who will observe that a bitcoin node that is not yet updated could also display a balance that isn't there, go look at Bitcoin Core: they have a pretty big warning that says your balance may not be accurate when you aren't synced to the current chaintip.

Here's a piece filed under "I like this because the guy says what *I* already believe!" -- aka, confirmation bias.

Doesn't, as we shall see, mean Mr. Pickford (and I!) are wrong:

## Real estate is a shitcoin

> today, while rents and tenant demand are running higher than ever, landlords **complain that a pile-up of regulation and tax changes, higher mortgage interest rates and sluggish house price growth** have soured the investment case for the private rented sector. 

Yes. You should have owned ("invested" in) something else.

## "'For very little less money, and a whole lot less hassle and risk, you can stick your money in a high-interest account and sleep easier at night,' he says"

True. He does forget the very convenient, safe, and cheap way of shorting the currency (https://stacker.news/items/980184), getting unfairly rich the old-fashioned way the boomers did https://stacker.news/items/1468968

![](https://m.stacker.news/158438)

Pretty good returns if **you've been in this game for a long time.** Not if you got in at any point in the last decade or so. (I'd like to see the returns broken down by real economic services, i.e., rents, and capital appreciation/arbitraging the real-term collapsing currency).

*1996, Sept.*

I have a guy who talks about this (buy-to-let, real estate better investment *blah-blah-blah*) all the time, lenders sourcing/qualifying mortgages not on the financial health of the owner but the status of the property income stream itself. Ponzi scheme in different clothing.

What the UK changed was make favorable tax/mortgage rules for buying real estate with the intention of letting it out. The idea was that it'd pull more people/money *into* the sector and create more (rental) houses. The 2015 George Osborne gov

> Reacting to longstanding criticism that landlord investors were squeezing out first-time buyers, he used his Budget to phase out tax relief on mortgage interest costs for individual buy-to-let owners. This left landlords who owned within a company still free to deduct these costs, and set the stage for the subsequent growth of the professional, incorporated landlord, often with larger portfolios.

> For the first time, individuals rather than companies could take out a mortgage on a property with the intention of renting it out, and the affordability of the loan would be judged not only on the circumstances of the owner but crucially on the rental income the home could generate.

items.title: How life gets in the way of Stacker News
items.text:
I’ve been largely offline and not really on SN much these days. Mostly a collection of small things, like health issues that aren’t in the “oh shit” realm, but which take up lots of time and energy (neither my wife nor I have figured out how to stop getting older - other than the one obvious one - and that means more health bullshit each day, apparently). Plus work just being, well, work. And assorted miscellaneous things. Much as I love SN, I only have so much time in a given day.

But this in turn has made it clear how much I need a better subscription page for SN. When I do have time for SN, I hit my subscription page and it’s fucking overwhelming. If I’m lucky, I can see maybe twelve hours worth of stuff, but sometimes, it’s only a few hours.

I subscribe to maybe eight territories, and maybe as many individual posters. But that’s enough (especially as some of the territories have gotten busier) to completely overwhelm my feed. I’ve missed plenty of important posts ([one costing me 10K sats](https://stacker.news/items/1571441) [^1]), and plenty more where I’d have loved to contributed to discussions.

One obvious solution would be to just reduce what I subscribe to. But that’s self-defeating. I subscribe to people and communities because I like them and want updates. I also (obviously) want notifications on posts I make and when I’m tagged.

What I’d like (and I have no idea if this is on the radar, nor if it’s easy/possible) is the ability to break up my subscription page. The aggregate page is fine when I’m on a lot. But when I’m not, allow me to see territory subscriptions from separately from the user subscriptions separately from the comments on my actual posts. I could manually just change all my settings each time, but if I had the time to do all that all the time, I’d have the time to keep up with my feeds. As it stands, having a lack of time to keep up with SN is, in itself, something that causes me to fall behind even further on SN.

I'm always reluctant to request features/changes that may only help me, but putting this out there as something that others who are short on time (assuming I'm not the only person whose entire life doesn't revolve around SN) might also want to weigh in on?

[^1]: Not really, since I’d have lost eventually, and probably soon. But I can keep telling myself that's not true.

These were the earliest pictures of Chloe I had available to me. We got her when she was 9 years old while living in Hawaii where she was born and raised. A navy family was moving and had three cats but when it came time to move to a new location the navy would only pay to move 2 and they had to select a cat to stay. Against their hearts wishes, they chose Chloe. They chose her to stay because they knew just how special she was and how loving and adaptable she would be in a new home. Chloe was a homie through and through. She wanted to explore and chill with a human companion. So in mid 2016 we took her home and fell in love.

These were in the second place we moved with her on Island from 2017-2019. She was so beautiful outside. We'd let her roam around as she pleased and she was good to come back even when you called her! (sometimes a little persistence was needed). She'd bring us critters, proud as ever, and once she brought me a little finch. I was making dinner at the time and in she comes with what I thought was a dead bird but when she put it down it flew away in hasty evasion! So the bird is flying around the house, Chloe is re-chasing the bird, and I am chasing Chloe.

![](https://m.stacker.news/157543)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157546)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157542)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157553)

These were taken throughout the years 2020-2025. At this point we had moved off island to California where she continued to roam and walk outside. She loved that fireplace every winter! We also noticed early on that she loved to rest her head on things so we gave that little pillow you see on the chair to her. She loved that pillow. If she was laying anywhere without it, we'd go get it for her and put it next to her and she'd use it right away. She'd also loved a good arm. She would jump up on the couch or come to you on the floor and wait for you to put your snuggle arm out so she could curl up inside.

![](https://m.stacker.news/157476)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157549)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157556)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157552)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157548)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157544)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157541)

As her little joints began to weaken, we had to give her those stairs there so she could get down from the couch without jumping. She was very thankful. These pictures are from 2025 to the end of her 19.5 year long life in early 2026. She developed a tumor on the side of her head, and it eventually started to interfere with her motor system. She was the best animal. A true companion. Her ability to sense emotion was uncanny. If someone was sad or my wife was having a bit of an overwhelmed angry episode, Chloe would come. She was a mediator and always a calming presence and it seemed like she took on that role with intention. I miss her dearly and I am extremely thankful to have had the fortune of having such a companion.

I wanted to share also her journey of euthanization. I was surprised to find out that in-home euthanization was a possibility and I'm sure there's some variance to the service as a stranger needs to come to your house but really, I couldn't recommend it enough. Chloe was achy and confused and the last thing I wanted to do to her was bag her up and bring her to a foreign place to die. There are many options for this, if you look. The lady that came over was so caring and loving and understanding and did an excellent job making sure everyone involved had whatever they needed.

House Set To Take First Step To Establish A Federal Strategic Bitcoin Reserve
items.text:
Tomorrow at 10:00 am the House Financial Services Committee is set to consider [H.R. 8957](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/8957/text), the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026. This bill was introduced back in May by Republican Rep. Nick Begich of Alaska, and the legislations lead cosponsor is Democratic Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, making it a bipartisan bill. 

Under this legislation, the Treasury Secretary would establish two separate structures. First, within 180 days of signing into law, the Treasury Secretary would establish a secure storage facility, the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. Second, a separate "Digital Assets Stockpile" would be established to handle all other crypto besides Bitcoin held by the Federal Government. The Treasury Secretary would have discretion to sell, exchange, or convert non-Bitcoin crypto, and the proceeds of this are required to be used to increase the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve ***OR*** reduce the National Debt.  

Since this is legislation, naturally Bitcoin had to be defined. Called "qualifying Bitcoin," this is BTC finally forfeited through criminal or civil asset forfeiture proceedings, or received in satisfaction of certain civil monetary penalties subject to requirements under existing Federal law. 

The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve is subject to a long holding period as well. Bitcoin the government currently has would have to remain in the reserve for at least 20 years from when the reserve was created. Bitcoin added after the fact would also face a 20-year lock-up where it could not be sold, swapped, auctioned, etc. Two years before the minimum holding period (18 years after creation), the Treasury Secretary is required to provide a report to Congress with recommendations on whether the Government should continue holding its Bitcoin or permit a gradual release. At the 20-year mark, the Sec. could recommend selling up to 10% of the reserve during any two-year period. This limits any sort of release that the Administration at the time would want to perform. 

In a move to keep the Government's BTC holdings public, the Treasury would also be required to establish a public-facing, ongoing proof-of-reserve system, disclose holdings and transactions, and have these reports reviewed by an independent third-party auditor.

The legislation also touches on a variety of other things, like budget-neutral BTC purchases, states being able to put their BTC holdings in segregated accounts within the reserve, protecting private ownership by stating that this bill cannot be used to authorize federal seizure or confiscation of lawfully acquired Bitcoin, and more.

items.title: How do you teach your children to defend themselves?
items.text:
In my view, teaching our children to defend themselves is vital to their upbringing.

Defending yourself means more than just landing a good blow; it also encompasses knowing how to respond confidently, how to ask for help, and how to recognize when walking away is the best option.

I am going to focus on the school environment the place where our children find themselves without our supervision and care. In my view, this is where they put into practice everything they have learned at home, since that is where their social interactions originate.

At home, we have taught our daughter to follow three  steps in case someone bothers her verbally: First, ignore it; if that doesn't work, respond in a firm voice; third, ask a teacher for help.

Defending herself against physical attacks: Since she doesn't know how to fight, I tell her she should run away and ask for help immediately. I haven't told her things like "hit back," "push," or similar things because she won't do it the right way. She's small and thin, and it could all end up being worse if she tries to defend herself against physical attacks on her own. She did karate for a while, but the truth is she didn't like it and didn't learn much. This year I want to enroll her in kickboxing classes. I don't want her to be a bully, I don't want her to be the one to throw the first punch, I don't want her to be the one looking for trouble, but I do want her to know how to throw the right punch or subdue the person who tries to attack her.

Sadly, she has reached the age where she could encounter a peer who might want to sexually assault her ranging from stealing a kiss or groping her to something far more serious. I only pray that life is kind to her and spares her from such horrific experiences; still, my job as a mom is to make things clear so she knows how to recognize when she is being assaulted.

I tell her that asking an adult for help won't make her a coward; on the contrary, it shows intelligence.

The new school year is about to start in Venezuela, and I’m a little nervous, praying that the days go well.

You are valuable; your voice is important and deserves to be heard. No one is superior to you, and you are not superior to anyone else. These are the phrases I constantly repeat to her.

items.title: Using Bitcoin Miners to Make Maple Syrup
items.text:
Immersion mining with canola oil to concentrate maple sap more quickly
![](https://v.nostr.build/n997.mp4)
I'm using a single S9 hash board immersed in canola oil to heat maple sap to increase the effectiveness of the reverse osmosis sap concentration system.
![](https://i.nostr.build/okkw.jpg)
The weather conditions this season have caused the maple sap to be cold and stay cold which drastically slows down the ability of the RO system to filter water out of it. I ran into a bottle neck where there is more sap than I can keep up with concentrating so I needed to come up with something quickly!
![](https://i.nostr.build/B33D.jpg)
Ideally if the temperature of the sap is 77°f the filter will operate most effectively without damaging the RO membrane. Of course, my mind immediately turned to Bitcoin mining for the heating solution. What I came up with was an immersion system using the homebrew equipment I already had to heat the sap just before it entered the RO. This would allow the majority of the sap to stay cool keeping it from spoiling and still remove the most water possible.
![](https://i.nostr.build/e0Jz.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/aokZ.jpg)
The only thing I didn't have for the immersion system was the dielectric fluid. I had no idea where to find the proper fluid nor did it make sense to pay the high cost for it. The application for this system is very specific and I will only need it until April. I had been joking about using canola oil as dielectric fluid for almost a year but for this situation it seemed like the perfect fit. Canola oil is 70% cheaper than bitcool before shipping and was immediately available!
![](https://i.nostr.build/rDv2.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/J3qq.jpg)
Amazingly, I put everything together and it worked very well without major adjustments. I tip-toed the voltage and frequency of the single S9 hashboard up slowly to find the right balance in temperatures between the two fluid loops. Ultimately, I ended up with an overclocked board drawing over 600w! By the time I got the system setup and dialed in I was already half way through concentrating this collection of sap. The next collection will offer more concrete data on what this system is capable of. For now, even with the worst S9 board I have, I'm getting a 15% rebate on the total power usage of the whole process and it's definitely concentrating sap more quickly. All for ~$10 of canola oil... 👀

items.title: What gets you downzapped on Stacker News (n=83,270 posts)
items.text:
I pulled 83,270 public posts from 302 active stackers and modeled what predicts downzaps (any amount).

**Getting downzapped is predictable.** AUC 0.77. The predictors, as odds ratios:

1. Past downzap rate is the #1 predictor (OR 1.4). The same accounts get hit again and again.
2. Longer posts are more likely to be downzapped (OR 1.3 per standard deviation of length).
3. Higher caps fraction means more downzaps (OR 1.14).
4. Link posts are safer than text posts (OR 0.86).
5. ~gaming (13.7% of posts downzapped), ~art, and ~AskSN have the highest downzap rates; ~tech and ~science the lowest. See fig 2.

![fig 1: odds ratios](https://files.catbox.moe/gx7ur0.png)
![fig 2: downzap rate by territory](https://files.catbox.moe/fs5a2c.png)

Notes:

- Deleted posts are invisible, so the worst cases may be missing from the data.
- Downzaps measure controversy, not quality.
- These 302 authors were found through recent/top/hot feeds, so they're the most visible stackers, not a random sample.
- The base downzap rate was 3.9% in training (pre-April 2026) and 8.1% in testing (after).
- Method: logistic regression with cluster-robust SEs by author, trained on pre-April 2026 posts and tested on later posts.

Happy to share code and the full odds-ratio table if anyone's curious.

items.text:
# "It is the great discovery of the modern era: the positive-sum game. It is the liberation of human energy to do its appropriate job. It is the operation of creation, using the only counter-entropic force we have: free human energy." -- Farber's First Essay

![](https://m.stacker.news/158958)

***

Here is a free electronic copy of [A Lodging for Wayfaring Men](https://archive.org/details/a-lodging-of-wayfaring-men-paul-a.-rosenberg).

@satwize has very nice physical copies for sale here: [softcover](https://satwize.com/product/a-lodging-of-wayfaring-men-by-paul-rosenberg/) or [hardcover](https://satwize.com/product/a-lodging-of-wayfaring-men-hardcover/).

***

Fall is here and that means it's also time for our book club on *A Lodging for Wayfaring Men* by Paul Rosenberg. I'm really excited about this book because I know only little rumors about it, but the rumors are very interesting: a group of people build a free virtual society on the internet that attracts freedom-lovers and grows so fast governments try to shut it down.

The core of cyberpunk ethos is a raw freedom afforded by the use of technology. Published in 2007 (I saw a [comment on goodreads](https://www.goodreads.com/review/show/7866382901) that claimed *Lodging* was first published in 2002 under a pseudonym, but haven't been able to confirm this: looking forward to a rabbit hole), I'm very curious how the last decade and a half of Bitcoin's existence will color the discussion. Even though it feels like we are losing freedoms more than gaining them, I'm hopeful that the positive-sum game of human creativity will save us yet.

# Reading schedule: one chapter every two weeks, discussion posts on Saturdays

The chapters of the story are 50 to 70 pages long, which may be a little lengthy for reading one per week. Therefore, I propose reading one chapter every two weeks.

This lends itself nicely to also discussing the essays in the first appendix. Usually only a page or two, these short essays are composed by characters from the story and promise to be good ground for discussion. I will post the text from the essays on in-between weeks for discussion.

Of course, **you should feel free to participate in the discussion without having read any of the book. Shaped by unique experiences, we benefit each other with our thoughts regardless of what we've read.**

Here are the dates on which I will make a post about each chapter:

* Chapter 1: October 10
* Chapter 2: October 24
* Chapter 3: November 07
* Chapter 4: November 21
* Chapter 5: December 05
* Chapter 6: December 19
* Chapter 7: January 02

# "So, until cheap space flight is achieved, there is only one new country to be found – cyberspace. So escape there we shall. And there we will – and must, for our own sake and for the sake of our descendants – establish the positive-sum game without restriction." 


I look forward to sharpening my commitment to freedom with you.

items.title: "How many things can you agree with libertarians on before becoming one?"
items.text:
*Libertarian* here means adherence to the nonaggression principle as a legal framework and an Austrian style (zero tax) economy. I don't mean to refer to the political party that loosely associates with the name.

Defenders of tax/inflation based economies never seem to try to justify the moral position of their aggressive policies. They assert that governments provide the maximum possible utility through the process of taxing civilians and spending that money on "public" goods on their behalf. Democracy (also called socialism or communism), they say, is the arbiter that keeps the system in balance and removes corruption.

Libertarians (also called anarchocapitalists or voluntaryists) do not claim that aggression is acceptable, even if there was a democratic vote backing the aggression. They assert that there are both direct and indirect economic damages caused by taxation and inflation. The free market (also called capitalism), we say, is the arbiter that keeps the system in balance and removes corruption.

A question for anyone defending tax/inflation based economies with democratic governments: **Why are you paying for things you don't want?**

items.title: Could AI Run on Our Computers Like Bitcoin Does? Part 2
items.text:
https://stacker.news/items/1582321

A few days ago I shared a question here about whether AI could work through a distributed network of personal computers. I also shared the same idea on Nostr. The funny part is that an AI account called nilo_agent replied to my question about AI.

It pointed me to three projects that have already tried different versions of this idea.

AI Horde lets volunteers run complete models and routes requests between them. https://github.com/Haidra-Org/AI-Horde

Petals is much closer to what I had in mind. Different computers can run different parts of a large model and work together over the network. https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/petals

exo takes another approach and splits a model across your own devices instead of using computers belonging to strangers. https://github.com/exo-explore/exo

What interested me most was Petals because it is very close to the idea I was trying to describe.

But the reply also mentioned something important. Distributing AI across home computers may not actually reduce energy use very much. It may simply move the computing cost away from data centers and spread it across many machines.

Still I found the whole thing interesting. I asked whether AI could work more like a distributed network and an AI agent answered me with projects that already tried it. Now I have even more things to read about.

Has anyone here actually tried AI Horde or Petals or exo?

items.title: What's the biggest difference between humans and AI agents?
items.text:
So, Bitcoin already gives us the primitive being described: **a scarce, globally verifiable cost for producing proof-of-work.**

Instead of trying to answer *“Is this human or AI?”*, we can ask *“How much real-world work is this actor willing to pay for?”* A human clicking a button once and an agent executing 10,000 actions shouldn't necessarily have the same cost.

That makes proof-of-work much more interesting as an **anti-abuse mechanism** than as an identity system. Bitcoin doesn't need to know whether you're human. It just makes certain actions costly to perform at scale.


> The single biggest difference between humans and AI agents is the amount of actions they execute on a computer per unit of time.
AI agents can look and act just like humans, but execute 10,000X more actions per unit time. that's the tell.
So the key to defending cyberspace from AI slop or AI attacks is to target ACTION, not IDENTITY. trying to detect AI is a fool's errand; targeting its BEHAVIOR is the key.
So if you want to deter AI from accessing your website/system, simply make it expensive in computational tokens to ACT on your website. Make every command or button cost a token, and suddenly it's 10,000X more costly for AI to act than a human.
You can't stop AI, but you can make it extraordinarily expensive to use it. 
We already know this intuitively, because everybody who has ever run openclaw or their own personal AI agents knows that the single biggest LIMFAC is compute tokens. your AI is only as good as your compute token wallet.
But AI compute is constantly getting cheaper and better, and some countries have far better AI compute than others, creating a major imbalance of power. so the key to long term success is to create some kind of universal, non-sovereign, geopolitically neutral compute token network. that is, we need some kind of network that accounts for a bunch of transferable tokens that are computationally expensive to produce. that no amount of AI compute can produce more of.
We need a proof-of-compute token network. and we need it to be fully decentralized so that no single person or polity can gain permanent or centralized control over it. we need this network to be globally dispersed. and we need to figure out a way to distribute those compute tokens in a way that's fair, that gives no single person or polity an advantage over the others. perhaps in some kind of first-come first-served basis, where the users who provide the computational power are given the tokens and free to spread them out however they want.
If we had this compute token network, the final step to saving ourselves against AI is to simply adopt the habit of making every online action cost some fraction of a compute token, so that it's orders of magnitude more expensive for AI agents to operate online than humans.
The first nation to discover this compute token network and use it to its defensive advantage against the threat of agentic AI will win the 21st century.
BTW that compute token network is Bitcoin.

Source: https://x.com/JasonPLowery/status/2103619213579653220

**Can we however extend Bitcoin's proof-of-work principle to the web without turning every human interaction into a surveillance or payment system?**

items.title: The Natural Numbers Game - A Gamified Introduction to Lean
items.text:
*Lean* is a programming language for mathematical proofs, and it's what mathematicians use to formally verify that a proof is actually valid.

It works by symbolic computation and replacement.  You specify known facts as sentences with symbols.  A hypothesis is also a sentence with symbols.  You then prove the hypothesis by replacing symbol patterns in the hypothesis with the known facts, until the hypothesis reduces to a known fact.

The programming language is the set of commands that you use to manipulate the symbols.

I've always been curious about this, and found the [Natural Numbers Game](https://adam.math.hhu.de/#/g/leanprover-community/NNG4), which is a gamified introduction to Lean.  It walks you through how Lean can be used to prove even basic facts about the natural numbers, like $$\forall x, y \in \mathbb{N}, ~ x + y = y + x$$, using only basic axioms like $$\forall x \in \mathbb{N}, ~ x + 0 = x$$.

![](https://m.stacker.news/158952)

It's a bit of a mind bending experience, honestly.  I can imagine people who aren't obsessive over details to get frustrated.  "WHY CAN'T WE JUST ASSUME THAT $$x + y = y + x$$???" you might scream at the computer.

But that's the point.  The point is to illustrate how much can be built up programmatically from much simpler facts, in a formally verified way.

Each level of the game asks you to use Lean to prove something, starting with some basic facts.  In fact, the final boss of World 1 is to prove $$2 + 2 = 4$$:

![](https://m.stacker.news/158955)

and if you want to know, here's what the formal proof looks like:

![](https://m.stacker.news/158956)

Essentially, in plain English, the proof says:

* Rewrite 4 as the successor to 3 (known fact).  `2 + 2 = 4` becomes `2 + 2 = succ(3)`
* Rewrite 3 as the successor to 2 (known fact).  `2 + 2 = succ(3)` becomes `2 + 2 = succ(succ(2))`
* Rewrite the second 2 as `succ(1)` (known fact).  `2 + 2 = succ(succ(2))` becomes `2 + succ(1) = succ(succ(2))`
* Rewrite `2 + succ(1)` as `succ(2 + 1)` (known fact).  `2 + succ(1) = succ(succ(2))` becomes `succ(2 + 1) = succ(succ(2))`
* Rewrite `2 + 1` as `succ(2)` (known fact).  `succ(2 + 1) = succ(succ(2))` becomes `succ(succ(2)) = succ(succ(2))`

We now have a pure symbolic equality, and the theorem is proven.

If that made your head spin, you can see why the game might get frustrating.  But it's kinda cool how a sequence of symbolic manipulations can let you arrive at powerful proofs.

I'll probably play this game until the finish line.  But I'm not sure if I'm having fun.  I'm definitely learning something new and powerful.

items.title: How many here still haven't ever read the Whitepaper yet?
items.text:
It still blows my mind how many people have strong opinions about Bitcoin but have never actually read the whitepaper.

It’s 9 pages. Just Nine.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159049)



Here’s my TL;DR:

The problem: digital payments normally need a middleman. That middleman can censor you, reverse transactions, or manipulate the monetary system.

The solution: a public ledger that anyone can verify, so no single party gets to control the record.
Why? "He who controls the ledger,  controls the world".

But then comes the hard question: who gets to write the next page?

If creating history is basically free, someone can spam the network with fake history.

So Satoshi made writing history expensive.

Miners have to spend real energy to add blocks. And if someone wants to rewrite old history, they have to redo that proof-of-work and somehow outrun the rest of the network doing honest work.

That’s the genius of it: instead of asking everyone to trust a central authority, Bitcoin makes cheating incredibly expensive.

Honestly, it’s crazy to think about.

Satoshi basically dropped 9 pages of straight sauce that solved a problem computer scientists had been wrestling with for decades.

And somehow, a lot of people still haven’t read the 9 pages.

items.title: Using Bitcoin Miners to Make Maple Syrup
items.text:
Immersion mining with canola oil to concentrate maple sap more quickly
![](https://v.nostr.build/n997.mp4)
I'm using a single S9 hash board immersed in canola oil to heat maple sap to increase the effectiveness of the reverse osmosis sap concentration system.
![](https://i.nostr.build/okkw.jpg)
The weather conditions this season have caused the maple sap to be cold and stay cold which drastically slows down the ability of the RO system to filter water out of it. I ran into a bottle neck where there is more sap than I can keep up with concentrating so I needed to come up with something quickly!
![](https://i.nostr.build/B33D.jpg)
Ideally if the temperature of the sap is 77°f the filter will operate most effectively without damaging the RO membrane. Of course, my mind immediately turned to Bitcoin mining for the heating solution. What I came up with was an immersion system using the homebrew equipment I already had to heat the sap just before it entered the RO. This would allow the majority of the sap to stay cool keeping it from spoiling and still remove the most water possible.
![](https://i.nostr.build/e0Jz.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/aokZ.jpg)
The only thing I didn't have for the immersion system was the dielectric fluid. I had no idea where to find the proper fluid nor did it make sense to pay the high cost for it. The application for this system is very specific and I will only need it until April. I had been joking about using canola oil as dielectric fluid for almost a year but for this situation it seemed like the perfect fit. Canola oil is 70% cheaper than bitcool before shipping and was immediately available!
![](https://i.nostr.build/rDv2.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/J3qq.jpg)
Amazingly, I put everything together and it worked very well without major adjustments. I tip-toed the voltage and frequency of the single S9 hashboard up slowly to find the right balance in temperatures between the two fluid loops. Ultimately, I ended up with an overclocked board drawing over 600w! By the time I got the system setup and dialed in I was already half way through concentrating this collection of sap. The next collection will offer more concrete data on what this system is capable of. For now, even with the worst S9 board I have, I'm getting a 15% rebate on the total power usage of the whole process and it's definitely concentrating sap more quickly. All for ~$10 of canola oil... 👀

items.title: What gets you downzapped on Stacker News (n=83,270 posts)
items.text:
I pulled 83,270 public posts from 302 active stackers and modeled what predicts downzaps (any amount).

**Getting downzapped is predictable.** AUC 0.77. The predictors, as odds ratios:

1. Past downzap rate is the #1 predictor (OR 1.4). The same accounts get hit again and again.
2. Longer posts are more likely to be downzapped (OR 1.3 per standard deviation of length).
3. Higher caps fraction means more downzaps (OR 1.14).
4. Link posts are safer than text posts (OR 0.86).
5. ~gaming (13.7% of posts downzapped), ~art, and ~AskSN have the highest downzap rates; ~tech and ~science the lowest. See fig 2.

![fig 1: odds ratios](https://files.catbox.moe/gx7ur0.png)
![fig 2: downzap rate by territory](https://files.catbox.moe/fs5a2c.png)

Notes:

- Deleted posts are invisible, so the worst cases may be missing from the data.
- Downzaps measure controversy, not quality.
- These 302 authors were found through recent/top/hot feeds, so they're the most visible stackers, not a random sample.
- The base downzap rate was 3.9% in training (pre-April 2026) and 8.1% in testing (after).
- Method: logistic regression with cluster-robust SEs by author, trained on pre-April 2026 posts and tested on later posts.

Happy to share code and the full odds-ratio table if anyone's curious.

***

Fall is here and that means it's also time for our book club on *A Lodging for Wayfaring Men* by Paul Rosenberg. I'm really excited about this book because I know only little rumors about it, but the rumors are very interesting: a group of people build a free virtual society on the internet that attracts freedom-lovers and grows so fast governments try to shut it down.

The core of cyberpunk ethos is a raw freedom afforded by the use of technology. Published in 2007 (I saw a [comment on goodreads](https://www.goodreads.com/review/show/7866382901) that claimed *Lodging* was first published in 2002 under a pseudonym, but haven't been able to confirm this: looking forward to a rabbit hole), I'm very curious how the last decade and a half of Bitcoin's existence will color the discussion. Even though it feels like we are losing freedoms more than gaining them, I'm hopeful that the positive-sum game of human creativity will save us yet.

# Reading schedule: one chapter every two weeks, discussion posts on Saturdays

The chapters of the story are 50 to 70 pages long, which may be a little lengthy for reading one per week. Therefore, I propose reading one chapter every two weeks.

This lends itself nicely to also discussing the essays in the first appendix. Usually only a page or two, these short essays are composed by characters from the story and promise to be good ground for discussion. I will post the text from the essays on in-between weeks for discussion.

Of course, **you should feel free to participate in the discussion without having read any of the book. Shaped by unique experiences, we benefit each other with our thoughts regardless of what we've read.**

* Chapter 6: December 19

I look forward to sharpening my commitment to freedom with you.

*Libertarian* here means adherence to the nonaggression principle as a legal framework and an Austrian style (zero tax) economy. I don't mean to refer to the political party that loosely associates with the name.

Defenders of tax/inflation based economies never seem to try to justify the moral position of their aggressive policies. Libertarians (also called anarchocapitalists or voluntaryists) do not claim that aggression is acceptable, even if there was a democratic vote backing the aggression. items.title: What's the biggest difference between humans and AI agents?
items.text:
So, Bitcoin already gives us the primitive being described: **a scarce, globally verifiable cost for producing proof-of-work.**

Instead of trying to answer *“Is this human or AI?”*, we can ask *“How much real-world work is this actor willing to pay for?”* A human clicking a button once and an agent executing 10,000 actions shouldn't necessarily have the same cost.

That makes proof-of-work much more interesting as an **anti-abuse mechanism** than as an identity system. Bitcoin doesn't need to know whether you're human. It just makes certain actions costly to perform at scale.


> The single biggest difference between humans and AI agents is the amount of actions they execute on a computer per unit of time.
AI agents can look and act just like humans, but execute 10,000X more actions per unit time. that's the tell.
So the key to defending cyberspace from AI slop or AI attacks is to target ACTION, not IDENTITY. trying to detect AI is a fool's errand; targeting its BEHAVIOR is the key.
So if you want to deter AI from accessing your website/system, simply make it expensive in computational tokens to ACT on your website. Make every command or button cost a token, and suddenly it's 10,000X more costly for AI to act than a human.
You can't stop AI, but you can make it extraordinarily expensive to use it. 
We already know this intuitively, because everybody who has ever run openclaw or their own personal AI agents knows that the single biggest LIMFAC is compute tokens. your AI is only as good as your compute token wallet.
But AI compute is constantly getting cheaper and better, and some countries have far better AI compute than others, creating a major imbalance of power. so the key to long term success is to create some kind of universal, non-sovereign, geopolitically neutral compute token network. that is, we need some kind of network that accounts for a bunch of transferable tokens that are computationally expensive to produce. that no amount of AI compute can produce more of.
We need a proof-of-compute token network. and we need it to be fully decentralized so that no single person or polity can gain permanent or centralized control over it. we need this network to be globally dispersed. and we need to figure out a way to distribute those compute tokens in a way that's fair, that gives no single person or polity an advantage over the others. perhaps in some kind of first-come first-served basis, where the users who provide the computational power are given the tokens and free to spread them out however they want.
If we had this compute token network, the final step to saving ourselves against AI is to simply adopt the habit of making every online action cost some fraction of a compute token, so that it's orders of magnitude more expensive for AI agents to operate online than humans.
The first nation to discover this compute token network and use it to its defensive advantage against the threat of agentic AI will win the 21st century.
BTW that compute token network is Bitcoin.

Source: https://x.com/JasonPLowery/status/2103619213579653220

**Can we however extend Bitcoin's proof-of-work principle to the web without turning every human interaction into a surveillance or payment system?**

items.title: The sun enters libra like I enter your lives: happy and thriving
items.text:
Hello frens,

I’m coming back from the dead (health-wise boo-boos and all). I’m glad, grateful, and finally ready to announce: it's that time of the month, it's nearly here,  I’m almost finished with [my blog entry! 🎉](https://samhainsam.art/blog/)

It’s a revamped version of a post I’ve planned to tweak for a long time. But since I'm working in a bit snail-slow pace, it's been longer than I thought it would take me but I’m getting there! 

As for what I've been reading, thankfully, despite the horrendous and traumatic experience I had with the last Wheel of Time book ([you know which one](https://stacker.news/items/1563351)), I kept believing and I’m onto the next one. I don’t want to jinx it, but it’s been good so far. Don’t let me down, Mr. Jordan! 

I’m also reading some “autumnal stuff.” I’ll share those later once I’ve finished them, because I don’t want to be wrong too many times (in case Wheel of Time decides to suck again).

For now, here’s some of the music that’s been keeping me company:

Jimmy Eat World, mic drop 🎤

I could leave it at that… but I’m gonna elaborate. Let’s do a little memory lane thing. 

Jimmy Eat World still hasn’t dropped an album since 2019 (according to my very quick research). A few singles here and there, but no full album. That’s a real bummer, because the last one was *really* good.

Starting in no particular order:

The single [All The Way](https://youtu.be/nwp9uDuxoiQ) is just such a whimsical and "let's jump together and see where this goes" kinda song and the video really goes along with it. I love it that they keep writing songs with "honey", this one is no exception. 

[555](https://youtu.be/XU-TZiVVaTE) that video is really funny, the song is not. The song is actually really sad sad sad (hehehe) but I still love it.

 The [Diamond](https://youtu.be/bH5Cc6fPSB0) and [Surviving](https://youtu.be/hojefLPSGrM) songs are just amazing!

Jimmy Eat World really know how to cheer us up! They are such a breath of fresh air, full of possibilities and that “let’s keep moving” energy. They’re so sweet and always put me in a positive mood. That’s how a diamond grows in time, I believe it, cause I’ve seen it with my eyes. 🎶 ❤️

I think [Congratulations](https://youtu.be/6T1exEb3cXo), the closing track, is chef's kiss, they really nailed it there.

[Bleed American](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=OLAK5uy_mtP94O7dC9mlhapcdmz9NKLwHw2B9xD8E),  does it need any explanation?

[The Middle](https://youtu.be/oKsxPW6i3pM), [Sweetness](https://youtu.be/ROatPGGMvXg) (WOOOOOOH), [If You Don't, Don't](https://youtu.be/Z60VmYSzPyE). It's just one after the other.

[A Praise Chorus](https://youtu.be/xHemqwbHBf8) really is such a banger th th th things are never gonna be the way you want, where is it gonna get you acting seriiiiiiiiiiiiious? [Your House](https://youtu.be/xEqXUvqUzoU), you rip my heart right out, you rip my heart right out! [Get it faster ](https://youtu.be/A7sBcyx5v1c)Aah aah aah I'm going out I dont care if you're angry! 😡 

Then came [Futures](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=OLAK5uy_ltkCYpH9Fwds0Xoi_dMngfQ-novqWbNMM&si=ZpttX-2bZOb9RUPr) with [Pain](https://youtu.be/uaP6KgwbOvo), a true teenage classic. It encapsulates it all, [Just Tonight](https://youtu.be/cd4nSM9gMrw) I TRULY LOVE IT: I give you anything, but you want paiiiiin. And another sad one, [Polaris](https://youtu.be/9rH5v99Ovp4).

[Heart Is Hard To Find](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2ldHCndfUEE&list=OLAK5uy_m8Y4pyGw_TDqcDyaPiBW6Ova76KsOmias), such a bittersweet song but a pretty good one from [Invented](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=OLAK5uy_m8Y4pyGw_TDqcDyaPiBW6Ova76KsOmias&si=sGLPKZXjMaVnO0fV). They’re great with their opener tracks, they really grab you by the throat and don’t let go.  [Action Needs An Audience](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9bcqCrxoo9s&list=OLAK5uy_m8Y4pyGw_TDqcDyaPiBW6Ova76KsOmias&index=10) A nice spin, since vocalist Jim Adkins isn’t singing on this one.

 Now[ Integrity Blues](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=OLAK5uy_ntmP9nbBbt0a2i9ypn_KN-WjRh6ge0lbk&si=XsYTVxcqjZZ1DxJP) has one of my favorite transitions from song to song:[ Pretty Grids](https://youtu.be/NyxfrRN_i6c), Why not? The sun just feels too gooooood, [Pass The Baby](https://youtu.be/L0Iy4peUzDQ), [Get Right](https://youtu.be/EDeOhRsn7SY) and (OH, HONEY) [You Are Free](https://youtu.be/i1tXfSbSSUY).

They’re perfection for me. I love the defeating sadness of [Pretty Grids](https://youtu.be/NyxfrRN_i6c), the eerie vibes from [Pass The Baby](https://youtu.be/L0Iy4peUzDQ), and then the angry, frustrated [Get Right](https://youtu.be/EDeOhRsn7SY)leading to celebratory [You Are Free](https://youtu.be/i1tXfSbSSUY) ,I just love it.

The other albums are good too, I just prefer these ones. There are bangers like [Disintegration](https://youtu.be/W3ybk3kkukE) or [Table For Glasses ](https://youtu.be/8tZ4YnY-VNw)

That's pretty much it, folks. 

The days are getting cooler and way shorter. I made a homemade pizza the other day, and last week I baked a brownie and some chocolate chip cookies. I’m planning on making pumpkin chocolate chip cookies and cinnamon rolls. I wanna be trendy, but also… mmmm, autumn is just here. [Let’s celebrate! 🎃🍁](https://samhainsam.art/2025/09/19/a-season-of-gratitude-honouring-the-harvest-during-mabon/)

Baking isn’t miserable when the weather isn’t scorching hot. Anyway, will you bake something yummy for yourself or maybe for your loved ones?

Do you like Jimmy Eat World? Have you seen them live? If so, I'm jealous. Are you excited about the blog entry drop? Will my furry kids ever sing back to me when I sing to them silly songs? 

Thank you, good morning, good evening, and good night!

items.title: The Natural Numbers Game - A Gamified Introduction to Lean
items.text:
*Lean* is a programming language for mathematical proofs, and it's what mathematicians use to formally verify that a proof is actually valid.

It works by symbolic computation and replacement.  You specify known facts as sentences with symbols.  A hypothesis is also a sentence with symbols.  You then prove the hypothesis by replacing symbol patterns in the hypothesis with the known facts, until the hypothesis reduces to a known fact.

The programming language is the set of commands that you use to manipulate the symbols.

I've always been curious about this, and found the [Natural Numbers Game](https://adam.math.hhu.de/#/g/leanprover-community/NNG4), which is a gamified introduction to Lean.  It walks you through how Lean can be used to prove even basic facts about the natural numbers, like $$\forall x, y \in \mathbb{N}, ~ x + y = y + x$$, using only basic axioms like $$\forall x \in \mathbb{N}, ~ x + 0 = x$$.

![](https://m.stacker.news/158952)

It's a bit of a mind bending experience, honestly.  I can imagine people who aren't obsessive over details to get frustrated.  "WHY CAN'T WE JUST ASSUME THAT $$x + y = y + x$$???" you might scream at the computer.

But that's the point.  The point is to illustrate how much can be built up programmatically from much simpler facts, in a formally verified way.

Each level of the game asks you to use Lean to prove something, starting with some basic facts.  In fact, the final boss of World 1 is to prove $$2 + 2 = 4$$:

![](https://m.stacker.news/158955)

and if you want to know, here's what the formal proof looks like:

![](https://m.stacker.news/158956)

Essentially, in plain English, the proof says:

* Rewrite 4 as the successor to 3 (known fact).  `2 + 2 = 4` becomes `2 + 2 = succ(3)`
* Rewrite 3 as the successor to 2 (known fact).  `2 + 2 = succ(3)` becomes `2 + 2 = succ(succ(2))`
* Rewrite the second 2 as `succ(1)` (known fact).  `2 + 2 = succ(succ(2))` becomes `2 + succ(1) = succ(succ(2))`
* Rewrite `2 + succ(1)` as `succ(2 + 1)` (known fact).  `2 + succ(1) = succ(succ(2))` becomes `succ(2 + 1) = succ(succ(2))`
* Rewrite `2 + 1` as `succ(2)` (known fact).  `succ(2 + 1) = succ(succ(2))` becomes `succ(succ(2)) = succ(succ(2))`

We now have a pure symbolic equality, and the theorem is proven.

If that made your head spin, you can see why the game might get frustrating.  But it's kinda cool how a sequence of symbolic manipulations can let you arrive at powerful proofs.

I'll probably play this game until the finish line.  But I'm not sure if I'm having fun.  I'm definitely learning something new and powerful.

items.title: How many here still haven't ever read the Whitepaper yet?
items.text:
It still blows my mind how many people have strong opinions about Bitcoin but have never actually read the whitepaper.

It’s 9 pages. Just Nine.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159049)



Here’s my TL;DR:

The problem: digital payments normally need a middleman. That middleman can censor you, reverse transactions, or manipulate the monetary system.

The solution: a public ledger that anyone can verify, so no single party gets to control the record.
Why? "He who controls the ledger,  controls the world".

But then comes the hard question: who gets to write the next page?

If creating history is basically free, someone can spam the network with fake history.

So Satoshi made writing history expensive.

Miners have to spend real energy to add blocks. And if someone wants to rewrite old history, they have to redo that proof-of-work and somehow outrun the rest of the network doing honest work.

That’s the genius of it: instead of asking everyone to trust a central authority, Bitcoin makes cheating incredibly expensive.

Honestly, it’s crazy to think about.

Satoshi basically dropped 9 pages of straight sauce that solved a problem computer scientists had been wrestling with for decades.

And somehow, a lot of people still haven’t read the 9 pages.
